The Complete Guide to South African Mortgages for Foreign Buyers: Rates, LTV, Documents and Approval Process

2026.08.03 10 min read Scott Huang | Business Development Property Investment

For many Taiwanese investors, the first question about buying property in South Africa is: "Can I get a South African mortgage?" The answer is yes — South Africa's mortgage policy for foreigners is more open than many people imagine. But the application process involves many details, from South African Reserve Bank (SARB) regulations, FICA fund review, loan-to-value ratios to interest rates. Understanding these rules is key to deciding whether to pay cash or take out a loan.

This guide gives you a complete breakdown of the rules and process for foreigners applying for a South African mortgage — from the legal framework, eligibility, Loan-to-Value (LTV), interest rate structure, to the approval process and frequently asked questions — helping you make the financing decision that best suits you.

Key Insight: South African mortgage approval places great emphasis on "transparent source of funds" and "repayment capacity." Buyers who remit funds through approved SARB channels and comply with FICA fund review will enjoy a much smoother loan process. Can Foreigners Get a Mortgage in South Africa?

Yes. South African law does not prohibit foreigners from applying for mortgages. Whether or not you hold South African residency, you can obtain purchase financing through South African banks. However, banks apply stricter scrutiny than for local residents, mainly considering the following factors:

  • Source of funds: Must comply with FICA, providing complete income proof and source-of-funds records.
  • Repayment capacity: Banks review your global income and calculate your debt-to-income ratio.
  • Loan-to-Value (LTV): Foreigners can usually borrow 50-70% of the price, requiring a higher down payment.
  • Currency risk: A loan denominated in rand means actual repayment cost is affected by exchange rate fluctuations.

Interest Rate Structure for South African Mortgages

South African mortgage rates are benchmarked to the "Prime Rate," with banks adding or deducting basis points based on your credit rating and repayment capacity. The South African Reserve Bank's (SARB) monetary policy directly affects the Prime Rate and thus the cost of mortgages.

For foreign buyers, the following rate concepts are worth noting:

Rate Concept Description
Prime Rate The benchmark lending rate of major South African banks, indirectly steered by SARB policy.
Fixed vs Variable You can choose a fixed term or variable rate; foreigners usually opt for variable rates.
Foreign Buyer Markup Some banks charge a higher margin to foreigners without South African credit history.
Currency Cost Repayment is in rand; assess the medium-to-long-term direction of TWD vs ZAR.

Loan-to-Value (LTV) and Down Payment

South Africa's loan-to-value ratio for foreigners is usually between 50-70%, meaning you need a 30-50% down payment. This differs significantly from local residents who can often borrow 80-90%. Banks also determine the final loanable amount through "property valuation" and "income verification."

LTV 50-70%

Common LTV for foreigners, requiring a higher down payment to reduce bank risk.

Down Payment 30-50%

For a R 10,450,000 property, the down payment is approximately R 3,000,000 to R 5,000,000.

Worth noting: if you have sufficient capital, cash purchase is often more advantageous than a loan — beyond avoiding interest and currency risk, it gives you greater negotiation leverage and saves bank charges. DingYao provides a cash vs loan analysis tailored to your funding plan.

Required Documents for Foreigners Applying for a South African Mortgage

South African banks conduct stricter document review for foreign buyers. The following is a list of commonly required documents:

  • Passport copy: Valid passport and visa (if applicable).
  • Source of funds proof: Bank statements and exchange records from the past 3-6 months.
  • Income proof: Payslips, tax returns, or company financial statements (for self-employed).
  • Credit record: If you have no South African credit history, a home-country credit report can support the review.
  • Purchase contract: A signed Offer to Purchase.
  • SARB compliance documents: Documents related to the foreign currency remittance application.

The Approval Process for a South African Mortgage

From submitting an application to loan disbursement, the South African mortgage approval process generally proceeds as follows:

1

Submit Application

Submit the loan application and complete documents to the bank or broker.

2

Eligibility Review

The bank verifies income, credit, and FICA source of funds.

3

Property Valuation

The bank commissions a valuer to assess the market value of the property.

4

Loan Approval

Receive the formal loan approval letter and interest rate terms.

5

Transfer Disbursement

Upon transfer completion, the bank disburses the loan to the trust account.

The entire approval process typically takes 3 to 6 weeks, depending on document completeness and bank processing speed. With Crestline Advisory's execution support, document preparation and bank communication can be greatly simplified, avoiding delays caused by unfamiliarity with the process.

South African Reserve Bank (SARB) and Foreign Buyer Financing

Foreigners financing property purchases in South Africa must note SARB's currency and exchange control regulations. Purchase funds should be remitted through approved channels, keeping complete bank records. If you later sell the property, funds can be remitted out of the country under conditions and subject to approval.

Key points of SARB regulations include:

  • Foreign currency remittance: Must be handled through SARB-approved financial institutions, declaring the purpose of funds.
  • FICA compliance: All sources of funds must be fully explainable to ensure anti-money-laundering compliance.
  • Repatriation limits: Proceeds from property sales are subject to annual limits and approval procedures.

Cash Purchase vs Mortgage: What Should Foreigners Choose?

For foreign investors, choosing cash or a loan is not just about "can you afford it" — it involves a comprehensive consideration of capital efficiency and risk.

Comparison Cash Purchase Mortgage Purchase
Capital Required Full amount upfront 30-50% down payment
Interest Cost None Paid annually per rate
Currency Risk Cost locked in once Long-term exposure to rand volatility
Negotiation Leverage Greater (faster close) Less (waits for loan approval)
Opportunity Cost Capital tied up, but can earn high interest Keeps capital flexibility

Frequently Asked Questions About Foreigners Applying for South African Mortgages

Can I get a mortgage without South African residency?

Yes. South African banks allow foreigners to apply for mortgages, but require a higher down payment and stricter source-of-funds review, with loan-to-value ratios typically between 50-70%.

What are South African mortgage rates?

South African mortgages are benchmarked to the Prime Rate, with the actual rate depending on personal credit and repayment capacity. Foreigners may pay a higher margin. You can use the Money Market 7.30% p.a. rate as a comparison benchmark for cash allocation.

How long does the mortgage process take?

From application to disbursement usually takes 3 to 6 weeks, depending on document completeness and bank processing speed. Professional advisory support can effectively shorten the timeline.

Should I pay cash or take a loan?

It depends on your capital and investment goals. If you have sufficient capital and seek cost certainty, cash purchase combined with high-yield Money Market allocation is often the better option; if you want capital flexibility, a loan is a viable choice.
